sections.body: Hourglasses are one of the best ways to track time in the strange Underworld. Even then, adventurers will notice that time flows curiously. An hour in the Underworld might be a day in the City.

sections.title: Iron spike
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Iron spikes can be used to wedge doors closed, serve as pitons for climbing, or be driven through the heart of the undead. (Stackable 6 per slot)

sections.title: Lantern
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Lanterns provide **bright light** to the person holding them and **dim light** for everybody else in the guild. Lanterns are lit by oil, which must be carried separately. Lanterns shatter when they are dropped. You can tie a lantern to your belt, but if you take a Wound the lantern shatters and you’re covered in oil. A lantern can **flicker** 4 **times** before their oil is used up ([[06 - Chapter 6 - The Crawl Phase#Flickers|Flickers]]).

sections.title: Lard
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Lard is the fat of a pig. It burns well, can be used as a grease to lubricate tools and surfaces, and can even be used as soap. You can also eat it like a ration in a pinch to keep from starving.

sections.title: Leeches
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Leeches draw out bad blood and let good yellow phlegm and bile reign in your poisoned body. You can apply leeches to another adventurer with the Use an Item Camp Action. If you do so, draw a card. If you draw a Swords or Pentacles card, nothing happens. If you draw a Cups or Wands card, the leeched adventurer counts as having burned 2 **charges to cure an affliction** ([[06 - Chapter 6 - The Crawl Phase#Afflictions|Afflictions]]).

sections.title: Lockpick
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Lockpicks can be used to pick a lock with a successful **test of Pentacles**. If you fail, one of your lockpicks breaks. (Stackable 6 per slot)

sections.title: Manacles
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Manacles are used to restrain people, usually to haul them back to the City for a reward.

sections.title: Mirror
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Mirrors are kept by those still trying to keep up a semblance of hygiene, or just to reflect a monster’s dread gaze back onto itself.

sections.title: Musical instrument
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Musical instruments are often carried by adventurers, as song keeps campfires merry in a dark and oppressive environment. These could be lutes, harps, flutes, viols, drums, or anything else found in the Wide World.

sections.title: Oil
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Oil, usually carried in a flask, is used to fuel lanterns. It can also fuel other fires, or be used as lubrication. A flask of oil provides 4 flickers to a lantern.

sections.title: Pick
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Picks are tools used for digging. (Oversized)

sections.title: Pipe and pipeweed
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Pipe and pipeweed are a great way to relax, clear your mind, and make the camp smell nice. Smoking all of your pipeweed **clears the Stressed condition**.

sections.title: Pole, 10’
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: 10’ poles are helpful, too-long walking sticks that you can use to prod and poke for traps and hazards. (Oversized)

sections.title: Poultice
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body:
Poultices are bandages infused with healthful herbs. They have a few different uses:

- You can expend a poultice to try and save a character at **Death’s Door**. The injured character **test Wands**; this test has favor if the person applying it has a medical motif. If successful, the Death’s Door condition is cured and the character returns to consciousness. If it is a failure, the character dies. See [[07 - Chapter 7 - The Challenge Phase#Death’s Door|Death’s Door]] for the full rules.

- Poultices are also necessary for the use of the Chirurgeon talent ([[05 - Chapter 5 - The Four Paths#Cups talents|Cups talents]]).

sections.title: Quill and ink
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Quill and ink are necessary tools for the journey into literary fame.

sections.title: Ration
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Rations consist of hardtack, dried fruit, and dried meats. It might not be delicious, but it’s better than starving. Each ration contains a canteen with a day’s worth of water or swill alcohol.

sections.title: Religious paraphernalia
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Religious paraphernalia is a catchall term for the icons, amulets, or rosaries used to ward away certain types of undead or spirits. If brandished, **test Wands**. If successful, **Displace** one affected creature. During a Challenge, brandishing a religious icon is a Wands action.

sections.title: Rope
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Rope comes in lengths of 50’. Every adventurer worth their salt carries a bit of rope on them.

sections.title: Salt
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Expend a slot of salt to **turn hunted game into rations**. Salt also dries out oozes and jellies if thrown at them. This is treated as an **Attack**, and inflicts **two Wounds** to **ooze** monsters on a success. Every adventurer worth their rope carries a bit of salt on them.

sections.title: Shield
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body:
Shields come in a variety of styles and methods of construction, but are considered either light or heavy. **Shields take one of your hand slots**.

- **Light shields** are made from wood. They can absorb 1 Notch.

- **Heavy shields** are made of metal or similarly sturdy materials and can **absorb** 2 Notches.

In a Challenge, ties go to the attacker unless the defender carries a shield.

If you have a shield, you may replace your Initiative with any card from your hand as a miscellaneous action. Your old Initiative is discarded.

sections.title: Shovel
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Shovels are tools used for digging. Like picks. But different. (Oversized)

sections.title: Spyglass
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Spyglasses magnify things up to five times.

sections.title: Tent
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Tents provide shelter and comfortable sleeping for up to two people. Without a bedroll or tent, sleeping on the cold ground makes you Stressed. (Oversized)

sections.title: Tinker’s kit
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Tinker’s kits are metal-working tools and scrap metal. You can repair damaged equipment with a tinker’s kit by performing the Use an Item Camp Action to remove 1 **Notch**. Destroyed equipment cannot be salvaged in this manner. (2 slots)

sections.title: Torch
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Torches provide bright light to the person holding them and dim light for everybody else in the guild. Torches have a 50% chance to go out when dropped. Torches that are extinguished are almost impossible to relight. Torches can flicker 3 times before they’re used up ([[06 - Chapter 6 - The Crawl Phase#Flickers|Flickers]]).

sections.title: Wand of archwood
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body: Wands of archwood are ritual implements that allow sorcerers to focus their magical potential. If you have the Gramarye talent ([[05 - Chapter 5 - The Four Paths#Wands talents|Wands talents]]), you may use an archwood wand as a missile weapon to create blasts of magical energy up to a zone away.

sections.title: Weaponry
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body:
**Weaponry** includes any basic arms and ammo listed in the Weapons section on **the following page**.

- Silver weaponry is expensive, but silver is often useful against lycanthropes, spirits, and certain types of undead. Silver weaponry is soft and easily damaged, however. Silver weapons can only absorb 1 Notch before being Destroyed.

sections.title: Wolfsbane
path: An incomplete list of pretty things
sections.body:
**Wolfsbane** repels wolves and lycanthropes. If brandished, **test Wands**. If successful, **Displace** one affected creature. During a Challenge, brandishing **wolfsbane** is a **Wands action**.

> [!epigraph]
> “To train with the sword, first master sweeping. When you have mastered sweeping, you must master the way of drawing water. Once you have learned how to draw water, you must split wood. Once you have split wood, you must learn the arts of finding the fine herbs in the forest, the arts of writing, the arts of paper making, and poetry writing. You must become familiar with the awl and the pen in equal measure. When you have mastered all these things you must master building a house. Once your house is built, you have no further need for a sword, since it is an ugly piece of metal and its adherents idiots.”
>
> _– Kill Six Billion Demons, Tom Parkinson-Morgan_

sections.title: Weapons
sections.body:
Weapons come in a variety of flavors. Each weapon has a **special property** during a Challenge based on its type.

Most weapons are 1 slot items except for polearms (which take 2 slots). All melee weapons can be wielded two-handed for the purposes of the Two-handed Focus talent except for daggers.

**The weapon types are**:

- Axes
- Daggers
- Blades
- Flails
- Bows (Arrows stack 12 per slot)
- Hammers and maces
- Crossbows (Bolts stack 12 per slot)
- Polearms (2 slots)

sections.title: Axe
sections.body: Axes include all types of chopping weapons, such as battle axes, bardiches, or mattocks. When an axe Attack **takes down an enemy**, you may use the same **Attack value** against another opponent in the same zone.

sections.title: Blade
sections.body: Blades include all types of swords, from short swords to longswords. When you successfully **Riposte** with a blade, you **deal 2 Wounds instead** of 1 **Wound**.

sections.title: Bow
sections.body:
Bows are ranged weapons that use arrows. When wielding a bow, you gain access to the special **Aim** Challenge Action.

- Aim is a Swords action. Declare who you’re targeting and play your card facedown. When you next **Attack with your bow**, you may reveal the card and **add its value to your total Attack**.

If you are attacked with a melee weapon while wielding a missile weapon, the attacker has favor against you.

sections.title: Crossbow
sections.body:
Crossbows are mechanized ranged weapons with a locking mechanism to keep the bowstring taut. **All Attacks with a crossbow deal Piercing damage**. However, your crossbow must be reloaded and cranked as a miscellaneous action after firing.

If you are attacked with a melee weapon while wielding a missile weapon, the attacker has favor against you.

sections.title: Arrows and bolts
sections.body: You must keep track of your **arrows** and **bolts**. They come in quivers of 12 per slot. Any arrow that hits a target is Destroyed (your opponent breaks off the shaft in combat, the bolt head is blunted on bone, etc.). Any arrow that misses may be recovered after the Challenge. Use the Fletch Arrows Camp Action to replace Destroyed arrows/bolts.

sections.title: Dagger
sections.body: Daggers are short, bladed weapons that include stilettos, gladiuses, and dirks. Daggers deal **Piercing damage** against targets who are **unarmed, Rooted, or Tripped**. Daggers may be thrown to Attack targets in your zone without engaging them.

sections.title: Flail
sections.body: Flails include any flexible weapon, such as morning stars or ball-and-chain. Flail Attacks cannot be absorbed by shields and **always win ties with Initiative**.

sections.title: Hammer or mace
sections.body: Hammers and maces include any type of smashing weapon. When your Attack value is at **least** _twice_ that of **your opponent’s Initiative**, your hammer **deals** 2 Wounds instead of 1 Wound.

sections.title: Polearm
sections.body: Polearms are long-hafted weapons that include spears, halberds, and quarterstaffs. **Ripostes are interrupts** when wielding a polearm. (2 slots)

sections.title: Example City Phase
sections.body: Muddy and bloody, the Four Aces stagger back to the surface. The guild consists of Weela Longtoes the bug keeper (gnome, Path of Cups), Alisander the morbid necromancer (human, Path of Wands), and Lucind the archaeologist (troll, Path of Cups). They are well aware that there’s only three members of the Four Aces—they think it’s funny.

sections.title: Step 1. Death and taxes
sections.body:
**GM:** As you return topside, you are met at the gates of the Underworld by the All-Watch. By this point, you’re familiar with the red painted eye on their full-face helms. Do you all pay your taxes?

_Weela is carrying 120g total and an elephant idol statue. She erases 60g from her adventurer sheet._

_Alisander is carrying 26g, six rubies pried out of the elephant idol, and a variety of dire whale scrimshaws depicting a profane ritual. He erases 13g._

_Lucind is carrying 51g and an old, torn-up book titled Ye Gorgonic Ecstasies. She erases 25g._

_After pausing for a moment for everybody to do their bookkeeping, the GM continues to facilitate the rest of the phase._

sections.title: Step 2. Noteworthy deeds
sections.body:
**GM:** OK, where’s your guy’s guild roster? What noteworthy deeds did you accomplish this delve?

_At the start of the City Phase, the guild has 2 Fame. When the guild arrives at the surface, the GM picks up the guild roster and erases the oldest deed accomplished (reducing their Fame to 1). Each guild member brainstorms a little._

**Weela:** Well, we successfully stole the eggs from that basilisk, which is pretty impressive.

**GM:** Definitely.

_Weela updates the guild roster. This sets their Fame back to 2._

_Alisander thinks a little bit and doesn’t have anything meaningful to contribute._

**Lucind:** We learned about the primordial elephant people by investigating the ancient elephant shrine. I don’t think anybody in the City knew anything about the elephant people before us.

**GM:** Hmm. I mean, I agree that this is interesting lore and new information, but it’s probably not noteworthy.

_The guild remains at Fame 2._

sections.title: Step 3. City Events
sections.body:
_The GM draws from the major arcana deck and consults the City Events table. They draw the Hanged Man \[XII], which gives a rumor:_

_A fallen star dwells on an island in the Boundless Moat, and his daughter came with him into exile. Both star-beings struggle adorably with human culture. The star wishes for someone to marry his daughter. As a dowry, the star will grant a wish to anybody who marries her. However, the daughter will interpret the wish. It would be wise to keep her happy unless you want the wish to go sour._

_The GM makes a mental note of this._

sections.title: Step 4. Turn in contracts
sections.body:
**GM:** OK, step 4—contracts. You have the eggs you were hired to get. Are you going back to Hugo Underhill, the master of the Malign Menagerie?

**Weela:** Yes! Absolutely. I have the eggs in hand and grin real big when we see him.

_The guild delivers the six basilisk eggs they managed to procure and are paid 50g per egg. Per their guild roster, the guild splits the loot evenly—a cool 100 gold apiece._

_The GM role-plays Master Underhill’s delight at this new addition to his menagerie. Master Underhill goes on to tell the guild about a rumor that he’s heard concerning a fallen star and star-daughter dwelling in the Underworld, and their purported wish-granting capabilities._

_Because they fulfilled a contract, each guild member gains 1XP._

sections.title: Step 5. Upkeep
sections.body:
**GM:** OK, you just got paid. What upkeep level is everybody going to get?

**Alisander:** I have some things I want to sell first.

**GM:** Sure.

_During this step, each adventurer tries to liquidate their assets by selling them at the Omphalic Market._

**Alisander:** I have six rubies and some dire whale **scrimshaw**.

**GM:** Remind me where you got the rubies?

**Alisander:** From the elephant idol.

**GM:** Right, right.

_The GM had noted the prices these treasures would bring in their notes, and quickly looks them up._

**GM:** OK, Alisander the scrimshaw goes for 20 gold and the gems are 30 gold each. That’s, uh…

**Alisander:** 200 gold.

**GM:** Thanks. Anybody else?

**Weela:** I want to sell the elephant idol.

**GM:** A merchant will give you 150 gold for it.

**Lucind:** What about this book I got? **I’ll** sell it.

**GM:** A bookseller appraises this as a modern volume merely meant to look ancient. She offers you 3 gold in a condescending way.

**Lucind:** Eh. I’ll just keep it. Maybe I can sell it to **someone stupider later**.

**GM:** OK. Upkeep?

**Weela:** Common.

_Weela pays 50g for common upkeep. She refills her pack with items from the impoverished and common equipment lists._

**Alisander:** Alisander is flush with cash. He’s going to live the life of luxury that he’s accustomed to.

_Alisander pays 100g. He refills his pack with anything from the Omphalic Market’s lists._

**Lucind:** I’m just going to save my money. I’m not spending anything on upkeep.

**Alisander:** I’ll pay for you if you want.

**Lucind:** No, that’s okay. I’m in pretty good shape, **actually**.

_Lucind doesn’t pay anything so is destitute. She starts the next Crawl Phase Stressed and buys nothing during this phase._

sections.title: Step 6. City Actions
sections.body:
**GM:** What City Actions does everybody do?

_Weela has been cultivating a species of dream moths in the City. She has brought back some rare flowers that she wants to feed the dream caterpillars. This has been an ongoing Support action. The GM has (secretly) determined that hatching the dream moths requires six steps of Support._

**Weela:** I want to feed the flowers I found in the Spires to my **dream caterpillar colony**.

_Using flowers found in the Underworld is clever, but the GM thinks that some gold should also be spent. They lower the cost of the Support action as a reward for the flowers._

**GM:** OK! Sure. The flowers are a good idea. You’ll also need to spend 10 gold for basic maintenance in terms of water, care, and space.

_Weela pays the cost and adjusts her gold totals. The GM updates their notes that Weela has taken another Support step on her moth project._

**Lucind:** Because I’m destitute, I’ll Beg and Busk.

**GM:** What does that look like for you?

**Lucind:** Well, I’m primarily an academic, so I’m going to stand on the City’s squares and rant and rave about academic subjects.

_Everybody has a pretty good laugh at this image. Weela and Alisander both have the ally Bond with Lucind, so Lucind’s player charges her Bonds with those two characters._

_Lucind draws from the minor arcana deck and gets a Knight of Swords. Since knights have a value of 12, she adds her Wands 1 for a total of 13 gold in donations from her public performance._

**GM:** Alisander?

**Alisander:** I’m going to Prepare Components.

_Alisander chooses the spells Brainfever, Control Undead, and Necromancy. He writes these components down on his adventurer sheet, with each component taking a slot._

sections.title: Step 7. Plan the next Crawl
sections.body:
**GM:** OK, so everybody has their actions done. Uh, let’s see. You all meet back up at a tavern. Do you want to go back to the Rat Cellar?

**Weela:** Ha ha, yes yes.

**GM:** OK, you descend the familiar crumbling stairs down into the basement bar. You get your cups and pull yourself a draft of the terrible, licorice-smelling liquor called rat’s milk. The same unsavory characters as always are there—arm wrestling, getting in spitting contests. There’s a job board in the corner. A big rat is gnawing on the cork of the board. What do you all do?

**Lucind:** I go over, try and pet the rat, then read the **job board**.

_The GM has pre-constructed a table of contracts. They draw 5 cards and read the corresponding contracts to the guild._

_The guild role-plays together. None of the contracts sound particularly appetizing to them for one reason or another. They did not complete Alisander’s quest last Crawl, so they will continue pursuing that goal. They briefly discuss what they think their leads are. The guild decides to try to go towards the Sepulcher of Titans dungeon._

sections.title: Step 8. Restock the Underworld
sections.body:
_After the session, the GM opens up their notes document and goes into their random tables—specifically, their Meatgrinder table and their City Events table._

_They delete the entries on the Meatgrinder table that have been drawn. After thinking a little about how the factions in the Underworld have changed because of the guild’s actions, they write some new Meatgrinder entries._

_They delete the old City Event rumor about the star-daughter. They write a new rumor based on the Meatgrinder entries they just wrote._

_The GM looks over their maps and makes sure they’re all up to date._

_In general, the GM doesn’t create new “plot.” They just think about the environment and make notes about potentially interesting consequences that could arise from the adventurers’ actions._

sections.title: Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering
sections.body:
> [!epigraph]
> “But see, amid the mimic rout A crawling shape intrude! A blood-red thing that writhes from out The scenic solitude! It writhes! — it writhes! — with mortal pangs The mimes become its food, And seraphs sob at vermin fangs In human gore imbued. While the angels, all pallid and wan, Uprising, unveiling, affirm That the play is the tragedy, ‘Man,’ And its hero the Conqueror Worm.”
>
> _– Ligeia, Edgar Allen Poe_

Dragons are a mystery. Dragons make dungeons full of magical traps. No one knows why. Dragons do not speak the common language, and attempts to communicate with them have driven sorcerers insane. They may not be evil, but they are so far away from humanity that you might as well call them such.

Mesi, the ancient philosopher, theorized that dragons domesticate and cultivate humans in the same way humans cultivate cattle, and no modern discussion of dragons fails to bring up (and usually disagree with) this curious point. The fact is, nobody knows much about dragons. (Dragons steal princesses, too. No one is sure why, either.)

sections.title: The GM’s Manifesto
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> A game is all about decisions. That is essentially what every game is, whether it's a traditional game like poker, or a board game, or an RPG.

A role-playing game’s _play_ happens via discussion. The GM describes things, the players ask questions, the GM elaborates, the players describe things, the GM asks questions, the players elaborate, and the process repeats. It’s a back-and-forth—asking questions and answering them. During this exchange, the GM and the players make decisions. This is what’s fun about RPGs.

Therefore, your job is to create interesting decisions for the players. Some advice to this end:

- Create environments that incite interesting decisions

- Create characters and factions with interesting motivations

- Describe the environment fully, engaging sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch

- Act in good faith by speaking generously

- Referee player actions fairly

sections.title: Create meaningful exploration
sections.body:
Decisions in an RPG should be interesting, not arbitrary. It is essential that, during the Crawl, you provide meaningful choices so that exploration is both fun and engaging.

An empty hallway with two branching paths doesn’t give the players enough information to make an informed or interesting choice. A coin flip could determine the “best” way to go. However, you could put Cant graffiti on the walls of the right path that reads: “Undead ahead! Do not enter! Turn back! All is lost!” If the players listen at the left path, they could hear the distinctively peacock-esque cry of the cockatrice. Now the players have information to make a decision: would they rather face a cockatrice or the undead? What are they most prepared for? Could they lure the undead towards the cockatrice?

Broadcast dangers. Hide treasures behind clues that make players feel clever. Create meaningful choices so that your players can make informed decisions.

sections.title: Create engaging personas
sections.body:
The Underworld and the City should both be full of memorable characters with their own interesting motivations. Each of the GM’s characters has a personality defined by their likes, dislikes, wants, and needs.

In the same way that dangers should be broadcast, so should your characters’ personalities. By clearly showing what a character’s likes and dislikes are, players will be given opportunities to role-play meaningfully.

The Underworld is deadly enough that not every single denizen needs to be hostile. The Disposition rules ([[06 - Chapter 6 - The Crawl Phase#Social Encounters & Disposition|Social Encounters & Disposition]]) make sure that players have a fair shake when encountering new characters. Give players opportunities to gather information, make unlikely allies, and take part in factional intrigue.

sections.title: Engage the senses
sections.body: Meaningful exploration only works when the players have a good sense of what is going on. Players need you to tell them as much information as possible about the environment they are acting within. Paint pictures with your descriptions, actually sketch out rooms when mental pictures are difficult to conjure, and be vivid about all five senses. Don’t leave out any salient details about things that players can see, hear, feel, or smell.

sections.title: Speak generously
sections.body:
Don’t fall into the trap of thinking that half-secrets and hints are interesting. Information-sharing games are only fun when information is actually shared. Maybe the information comes with a price (“You’re not sure if the dragon is truly sleeping or only faking it. You’ll have to move closer to get a better look at him…”), but when it comes time to pay the piper, give the players as much information as you can. “Gotcha” moments are not fun.

This is particularly true when players bid lore. If you accept a lore bid, you have a social obligation to speak generously to the player and give as much information as is appropriate.

sections.title: Be a fair arbiter
sections.body:
> [!sidebar] Arbitrating Rules Questions
>
> What should be done if there is a rules dispute during gameplay? One of the GM's duties is to settle these questions and decide how the rule should be played. If you're still learning the game, you might want to look them up every time until the flow of narrative and mechanics feels natural. If you have the rules down pretty well but encounter a speedbump, we offer this suggestion: decide in favor of the players and look up the rule later. Don't slow down a fun combat with page turning. Just make a temporary rule that is beneficial for the players and ask your best rules lawyer at the table to look it up after the combat is over.

Let player decisions carry weight. If the players come up with ideas that should work, you don’t even need to touch the cards. Their plan can simply work. What makes sense comes before the rules.

At the same time, don’t pull punches. Victories are only valuable if defeat is a real possibility. You are neither the players’ antagonist nor their friend. One of your roles is to be a neutral interpreter of the _physics_ of the imaginary world.

There are random elements. Interpret them judiciously. As much as possible, make the mechanics visible. Say what you’re doing, what the players are testing fate for, and what the results will be.

As the GM, you can give difficult situations to the players with _no idea how to solve them yourself._ The players will surprise you with their ingenuity and **problem-solving skills. When they come up with something surprising and cool** that _should_ work, let it work.

> [!epigraph]
> “Deep in the human unconscious is a pervasive need for a logical universe that makes sense. But the real universe is always one step beyond logic.”
>
> _– Dune, Frank Herbert_

sections.title: Running the Crawl Phase
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> The standard flow of the Crawl is as follows:

The players declare where they intend to go. If the guild begins this phase by leaving the City, they declare which entrance to the **Underworld** they will use. If the guild is in the Underworld, they declare the direction they move (e.g., “We’ll go towards room 12 to the east.”)

- The GM draws a card from the major arcana for the [[06 - Chapter 6 - The Crawl Phase#Meatgrinder|Meatgrinder]].

- The GM asks, “What light do you have?

Based on what the players can see, the GM describes the room’s contents in addition to the Meatgrinder results.

The GM asks, “What do you do?”

- The players ask the GM questions about the environment.

- The players describe their actions.

- To help adjudicate, the GM asks, “What do you have in your hands?”

The GM arbitrates the results of the players’ actions. The GM calls for tests of fate when the situation is tense and failure is interesting. This entire process repeats.

sections.title: Creating your Underworld
sections.body:
> [!sidebar] Homebrewing
>
> Running a game is sort of like cooking. The first few times you do it, you adhere judiciously to a recipe. However, the more you cook, the more that repetition, experimentation, improvisation, and restriction reveals the methodology and chemistry that underlies the recipes.
>
> This game is a complete package but it is just a recipe. It has an underlying chemistry that produces a particular taste. The more you play it, the more you’ll understand how the parts and pieces work together. Once you do, you’ll understand how to change parts of it to better suit your tastes. The game is better when the book is not the authority; rather, authority is given to the GM and the general will of the table.
>
> If this book mentions something in passing like, say, lycanthropy, we haven’t felt the need to give you paragraphs and paragraphs of crunch on the subject. RPGs have been going on for a few decades now. There’s information out there. Find some time between sessions to create some lycanthropy rules that you like. Make the lore work for the game world that you’ve made. Get player buy-in about the idea and get everybody excited about it.

You own the act of mapping the dungeon, inventing the stats for monsters, designing traps to be overcome, and hiding rewards. _His Majesty the Worm_ front-loads this work. Before you start running a game, you’ll want to sit down and sketch out the entire Underworld megadungeon that you’ll be using. Appendix E deals with generating your Underworld megadungeon.

Doing this work over the course of one or two Sunday afternoons frees you from doing weekly game session planning. You’ve done the hard work already. The City Phase will be your trigger to keep your dungeons fresh: this is when you think about how the players have changed the situation in the Underworld, update your notes accordingly, and create new Meatgrinder entries to replace the ones the players have already seen.

sections.title: Creating a soundscape
sections.body:
You can provide a sense of consistency and theme for the different dungeons of your Underworld by building a bespoke playlist. Associate each level with a specific song. When the players enter a dungeon, play its theme song on a loop. (Choosing a music player with a looping option is important. Spotify works well.)

You can also have theme music for the beginning and ending of a session, for Challenges, and for recurring GM characters.

Video game music works well for this purpose. It’s designed to fade into the background and create an atmosphere. Be aware that your players may indelibly associate the music with that particular video game, taking them out of the _His Majesty the Worm_ experience. Choose your favorite music from obscure games or games you know your table hasn’t played overmuch.

_Your mileage may vary._ Some players find any music—even music without lyrics—to be very distracting. Ask your table what they prefer.

> [!epigraph]
> “Wherefore each of you, when his turn comes, must go down to the general underground abode, and get the habit of seeing in the dark.”
>
> _– “The Allegory of the Cave,” The Republic, Plato_

sections.title: Creating interesting characters
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> It’s your job to portray characters with personalities that are evocative, strange, conflicting, and clearly broadcast. This is true for all creatures that you control, no matter how monstrous!

Each character you introduce should have a personality defined by their dislikes and **likes, wants** and **needs**.

- **Dislikes** are gates to the character’s heart.

- **Likes** are the key.

- **Wants** are aspirational character desires.

- **Needs** are foundational character desires.

Understanding a character’s personality allows you to arbitrate the guild’s attempts to bargain with them fairly. Reference the Dispositions see [[06 - Chapter 6 - The Crawl Phase#Social Encounters & Disposition|Social Encounters & Disposition]] for role-playing guidance.

sections.title: Dislikes
sections.body:
Dislikes trigger negative Dispositions like distaste or anger.

- These triggers can be behaviors (“lying”) or traits (“all elves”).

- GM characters won’t bargain with adventurers that they dislike.

sections.title: Likes
sections.body:
Likes trigger positive Dispositions like trust or joy.

- These triggers can be behaviors (“sharing alcohol”) or traits (“good at music”).

- GM characters will bargain fairly with adventurers that they like.

sections.title: Wants
sections.body:
Wants fulfill the character’s wishes.

- Wants are discrete. They can be items (“enough money for a dowry”) or events (“marry the widow Prescott”).

- If a GM character is offered something they want as a bargaining chip, tests of fate to manipulate them are made with favor.

sections.title: Needs
sections.body:
Needs represent the status quo.

- Needs are abstract and essential (“for Baron Afanas to stay in power so the peasants continue to pay their taxes to me”).

- If a GM character’s needs are threatened as a bargaining chip, tests of Wands to manipulate them are made with favor but their Disposition will be a hostile one, such as anger or distaste. They won’t bargain again.

Contrasting or conflicting likes, dislikes, wants, and needs ensures that the players have multiple ways to interact with GM characters.

For instance, some mermaids might **like gossip** and **want to eat a man’s** eyes, **the tips of his fingers, and his privates**. A guild of men encountering mermaids are likely targets to be devoured. However, if the guild feed the mermaids juicy gossip instead, they might avoid a combat encounter.

sections.title: The blessing of chaos
sections.body:
Sometimes Meatgrinder events target random adventurers. Sometimes you can imagine a few equally reasonable possibilities and want some help making a fair decision. You can use the cards as a random oracle to help you make choices. Expose this randomness to your table. It will make you seem more “fair.” You can alleviate some of the harshest feelings of injustice by leaving an adventurer’s fate up to the cards.

Here are some tips for handling random events during the flow of gameplay.

sections.title: Events targeting an adventurer
sections.body:
Sometimes, a Meatgrinder event targets _one particular adventurer._ This should make sense in context: the first person in the marching order might blunder into the trap, whereas the last one in marching order doesn’t notice that their potion bottle is broken and leaking.

Sometimes, Meatgrinder events or an enemy’s attack targets a _random adventurer._ In this event, consult the top card of the minor arcana discard pile. The random effect will target the player whose path matches that suit. If you have multiple people with that path at the table, use the card’s value to choose between them in a quick way (e.g., odd is the first player to your left, even is the first player to your right).

sections.title: Events targeting equipment
sections.body:
You’ll notice that the adventurer sheet has four belt slots and twenty-one pack slots. These numbers were intentionally chosen.

If you need to target a player’s belt slot with a Meatgrinder event, glance at the minor arcana’s discard pile and note the top card’s suit for a random number 1–4.

- : First belt slot

- : Second belt slot

- : Third belt slot

- : Fourth belt slot

If you need to target an adventurer’s pack, glance at the major arcana’s discard pile instead for a number 1–21, based on the value of the card.

sections.title: What are you holding?
sections.body: There is one question that helps inform your adjudication of all other player actions: “What do you have in your hands right now?” **This is the most important question in your GM tool kit**. Anything an adventurer attempts might be hampered or helped by the answer.

sections.title: Example the first
sections.body:
**Player:** Can I climb the wall here and look over it?

**GM:** Well, the wall is made of crumbling brick, so sure, it would be easy. What are you carrying?

**Player:** I'll leave my sword and shield on the ground.

**GM:** OK. So, you prop your sword and shield against the wall and start climbing the wall?

sections.title: Example the second
sections.body:
**Player:** OK, I want to try and pick the lock on the weird door with the face.

**GM:** Who has the light source? (A variation on “What's in your hands?”)

Player 2: I do. I'm standing guard by the first room to make sure nobody ambushes us.

**GM:** If you're trying to pick the lock but your light source is at the cavern's opening, you basically can't see what you're doing. That'll be disfavor for sure.

**Player 3: I'll** pull out my torch and light it off of Player 2's and stand near the locked door to provide light.

**GM:** OK, that works. Test fate with Pentacles.

The fiction of what an adventurer is holding gives you immediate context for the rest of the scene.

sections.title: How much treasure?
sections.body: You might ask “How much treasure should I give the players?” This is not the right way to think about it. Riches and life are both cheap, and can be quickly lost. Remember that the luxurious [[09 - Chapter 9 - The City Phase#^upkeep|upkeep]] in the City is 100 gold. Getting this can feel like a major reward. If players land a major haul, having a few City Phases where they live in the lap of luxury will reinforce the feeling that they had a major accomplishment. After that money is gone, they will return to more humble living.

sections.title: What can I see?
sections.body:
When a player asks what their adventurer can see, describe everything in the room that they could possibly see or notice. This gives players enough context to actually interact with the room in a meaningful way.

This information is filtered by a few factors, of course. An adventurer might not be able to see in the dark, but they could still hear their environment. They won't be able to see hidden or obscured objects (like a secret door or a thief hiding behind a curtain), but are free to search in more thorough ways.

Essentially, there are three levels of information based on how thoroughly an adventurer looks around them. No tests are required and no cards need to be drawn; the only thing that is tested is a player’s thoughtfulness while asking questions.

1. **Glancing:** This covers everything that can be perceived in an area by someone who has good light.

2. **Scrutinizing:** Gated, until the players ask questions. “Is the gargoyle made of stone?” “What color is the book?” “What are the pages made out of?” “Are the hinges inside or out?”

3. **Investigatory:** Gated, until the adventurers interact with the environment. “I try to twist the moose head. Does it feel like it has any give?” “**I’ll** pull back the tapestry. Is there anything behind it?” “I tap on the walls. Do they sound hollow?”

Information should only rarely be held back from the players. Be charitable in the information you give: the more information a player has, the more interesting choices they can make. So, even in a room with a secret door, the adventurer might feel a slight draft in the room that reveals that something is amiss. Or if there was a thief behind a curtain, they might hear a muffled cough for a moment, but then nothing.

sections.title: What do I know?
sections.body:
When a player asks, “Would my character know about X?” make a quick call on how obscure the question is. If the question is something their adventurer might possibly know, speak generously about the subject. If the question is obscure, ask the player if they have a motif they could use to bid [[02 - Chapter 2 - The Adventurer#10. Lore|lore]].

There are essentially two levels of knowledge.

1. **Obvious knowledge:** This covers stuff everybody knows and sets the general expectations of a situation. Giving players a lot of information makes sure that both players and the GM are on the same page and lets players make intelligent choices.

2. **Obscure knowledge:** Some specialist subjects are only going to be known to certain people. Obscure knowledge might include the habits of supernatural creatures, the likes and dislikes of specific people within an organization, or the metaphysics of the planes of reality. This information should only be given to players who **bid lore**.

If a player bids lore and you accept the question, give as much information on the subject as you know—just keep talking and riffing until you run out of material.

sections.title: Running the Challenge Phase
sections.body:
The Challenge rules resolve questions of timing between hostile forces in a fair and fun way. Actions like “We all run past the imps and slam the door” and “I want to shoot an arrow at the lich before they complete the ritual” are best answered by using the timing of the Challenge Phase.

The Crawl Phase can transition to the Challenge Phase and back organically. When there’s tension and a hostile situation does not seem resolvable with a single test of fate, call for a Challenge Phase. When the opposition is defeated, the outcome of the Challenge is clear, or the players want to retreat, transition back into the Crawl.

sections.title: Creating interesting locations
sections.body:
When possible, **Challenges should take place somewhere cool**.

Cool encounter spaces provide **potential energy—they** give the players (and the GM!) stuff to interact with. Scatter one or two interactable pieces of scenery across each zone, including dynamic **terrain**, **sensory information**, and **usable objects**.

sections.title: Terrain
sections.body: Create spaces that tell a story. Challenges often inhabit a liminal space, set between safety and danger, stable and unstable, solid and liquid, cool and hot, heights and depths. Exploit these contrasts.

sections.title: Sensory information
sections.body: An adventurer’s understanding of their environment is based on the limits of their senses. By default, the Underworld is a dark and difficult place. Place further restrictions on the guild’s vision, hearing, and other senses to provide additional challenges.

sections.title: Objects
sections.body:
Empty rooms are boring. Each space should be scattered with interesting items. Set pieces can be picked up, hidden behind, or smashed through.

| Terrain | Sensory information | Objects |
|---|---|---|
| A bridge over a chasm | Smoke near the room’s ceiling, choking or blinding tall characters | Hanging tapestries |
| A 45° collapsed obelisk | Fungus that extrudes choking spores, lights, or sounds when bumped into | Braziers of coals |
| Chains hanging from the ceiling | Fog near the room’s floor, obscuring short characters | Silk dressing screens |
| Icy floors | A colossal ringing bell, deafening all nearby | Tables and chairs |
| A climbable idol | Blinding light emanating from a bright red ruby | Bookshelves |
| Hanging chandeliers | The area is half-filled with murky water | Taxidermied monsters |
| Quaking floors | Illusory objects and creatures | Fountains |
| An oil slick | Shrieking wind, preventing flight or missile weapons | Weapon racks |

sections.title: Creating interesting battles
sections.body:
Your job as the GM is to keep the Challenge flowing. You track the Initiative count, lead discussions about rules, and make rule calls when players attempt different types of actions. And, importantly, you control the antagonists during the Challenge.

Here are some lessons learned during playtesting to help you create tactically difficult and rewarding Challenges.

sections.title: Gang up on the players
sections.body:
Players have more cards in total than the GM. They will act more often. However, you have an advantage when it comes to the number of antagonists.

- With multiple enemies, each action you use can target the same number of adventurers. If five goblins use the Attack action, this will affect up to five different adventurers.

- Enemies can also focus fire, attacking the _same_ adventurer. Use the rules for mobs see [[07 - Chapter 7 - The Challenge Phase#2. Play Initiative for each significant enemy|Play Initiative for each significant enemy]] to good effect.

- The GM’s “side” can often absorb more Wounds than the players.

The gimmick is that players feel cool as they mow down hordes of zombies or bandits or whatever. At the same time, it’s a war of attrition—the GM can **put** pressure on the players as they face hordes of enemies.

sections.title: Make minor actions as often as possible
sections.body:
You have much more freedom than players when it comes to card choice because you don’t have to worry about card suits. As such, take minor actions as often as possible.

Smart players will try to keep the monsters “stun-locked” with Roughhouse and various effects. Smart GMs will use Recover, which doesn’t have a requisite value—simply discard any lesser doom card as a minor action to keep your antagonists free and ready to act.

sections.title: Fight dirty, fight fair
sections.body:
Don’t pull punches, but fight fair. Don’t change your monsters’ stats halfway through a battle. If the players come up with an amazing plan and shove your big bad guy off of a tower, let it happen. Of course, what is good for the goose is good for the gander. If the players start shoving your Balrog off the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, you can pull their wizard off of it just as easily (if you have the appropriate card).

If the players are losing, they have a choice to make: stand and fight, run away, or talk their way out of it. The Disposition and Morale rules make sure that the players have ample opportunities to talk their way out of a fight at pretty much any stage.

sections.title: Creating interesting antagonists
sections.body:
Challenges that just consist of “smack the other guy dead” can be boring. Make fights with goals other than defeating the enemy. To this end, **create antagonists with potential energy**.

For example, if a Meatgrinder encounter simply lists “1–4 skeletons,” the Challenge Phase will consist of the antagonists whacking each other until one side expires from Wounds. However, if the Meatgrinder details, “1–4 skeletons in a **pit** that seem to be guarding a skeleton with a golden crown; the crowned skeleton is not moving,” the encounter gains more texture and raises several questions:

- Can the adventurers get the crown off of the king skeleton safely?

- What happens if they do? Does this trigger something?

- What is the story of these undead? How does it relate to this region of the Underworld?

- How can the pit be safely navigated by the adventurers?

As the guild moves through the Underworld, the potential energy from one antagonist will transfer onto another until eventually there is an explosion—with the players caught in the middle.

sections.title: Creating surprises
sections.body:
If things are beginning to get stagnant, introduce something that changes the Challenge dramatically. Let the potential energy transfer into **kinetic energy**.

Here’s a table to inspire ideas for different ways to shake things up. Glance at the top of the minor arcana discard pile for a random event:

| Card | Twist |
|:---:|---|
| I | The current conflict smashes down a nearby wall, connecting the current room to an adjacent one. What dwells in that room, and how will it interact with the current scene? |
| II | A wandering monster wanders into the scene. |
| III | An infantile wandering monster wanders into the scene. It imprints onto a random adventurer. |
| IV | A rival adventuring party, currently struggling with problems of their own, crash onto the scene. |
| V | Something in the current scene is revealed to only be an illusion. |
| VI | Something in the scene is revealed, with further investigation, to be something completely different. The orc is just three goblins in a trench coat. The gargoyle is just a statue. |
| VII | A secret passage is revealed, leading to hidden treasure or danger. |
| VIII | A chance blow rips open a backpack, causing two alchemical potions to crash onto the ground. As the two reagents mix, a terrible ooze begins to form, farting out magical clouds as it does. |
| IX | Disembodied spirits climb inside the bodies of nearby slain foes and reanimate them as flesh puppets. The spirits have their own agendas. What do they want? |
| X | A dropped torch or knocked over brazier starts a fire which quickly becomes a hazard as the area is filled with smoke and flames. |
| Page | The area becomes suddenly flooded with water/wine/sludge/something else. What is the source of this deluge? |
| Knight | The next time an adventurer is dealt a Wound, they are dazed. When they come to their senses, they distinctly remember a preternatural voice speaking to them. What is this divine revelation? Is it real? Or is there something going wrong in the unknowable space behind their eyes that’s undiagnosed? |
| Queen | Death shows up and stands quietly in the corner. He’s a few minutes early, but is willing to wait. |
| King | A stampede of doppelgangers barrels down the passage and accidentally bumps into the guild. They get all tangled up, tripping over each other. After the confusion, the party is substantially larger. Each player has at least two, but maybe as many as four new adventurers. Not even the players are sure who is who. Give them new adventurer sheets for their clones until things are sorted out. |

sections.title: Running the Camp Phase
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> Camping scenes are moments of relative calm within the frenetic journey of the Underworld. They are explicitly times for a guild to regroup, role-play with each other, and recover near the warm light of the campfire before moving on into the waiting darkness; a time for the whole table to breathe a sigh of relief.

The GM’s job is two-fold during the Camp Phase:

- Act as the master of ceremonies to make sure that the Camp Phase flows smoothly, adjudicating any rules questions that come up

- Inject color into the scenes of the encampment

The latter is done by asking questions. For the vast majority of the game, you have to be “on”: you describe the setting, interpret the Meatgrinder results, role-play various characters. The Camp Phase is an opportunity for you to take a break, too. Give some of the narrative work to players: ask them to describe their gear, how they set up camp, what sort of rations they’re preparing, etc.

When the adventurers break bread (step 2), you can provide some discussion prompts and ask for a small scene to be role-played out. Frame these questions as subjects the entire guild is discussing: for example, “You’re all discussing the worst injuries you’ve had. What are your scars and where did you get them?”

Whenever the players riff on these questions, they provide you free ideas. Take notes about what the players are talking about at camp. Use them to seed the content of the City Phase!

- Did a player riff a story about their childhood sweetheart? Create a special City event where she invites them to her wedding. Will they accept?

- Did a player mention their mother’s famous lemon tart? When they get back to the City, she’s mailed them one—a free ration for the next crawl!

- Did a player mention an old enemy? Place their enemy in the City. Next time they surface, she approaches them on the street and asks to bury the hatchet. How will they react?

Don’t fall into the trap of thinking that punishment equals good role-playing. Don’t go and kill old loves, parents, friends. Rather, draw these personas into the story and create flash points for the players to act.

sections.title: 50 campfire discussions
sections.body:
1. What’s special about your weapon?
2. What do you currently look like? Has adventuring torn or tarnished your once-pristine gear?
3. What’s your favorite personal possession?
4. What weird traits does your animal companion have?
5. Who were your parents? Are they alive?
6. What songs do they sing in your homeland?
7. What was your first adventure into the Underworld?
8. Would you rather eat a plate of maggots, or have a hundred maggots placed secretly in your food over the course of a year?
9. Do you have any tattoos? Why did you choose them?
10. Who was your first kiss?
11. When did you lose your virginity?
12. When was the first time you saw magic performed?
13. If you could learn another language, what would it be?
14. What monster was the scariest for you to fight? Why?
15. When did you learn how to swim?
16. What’s your favorite food?
17. What’s something you’re afraid to lose?
18. What do you miss about your homeland?
19. Kill/marry/fuck your other guild members?
20. What was your first pet? What was his name?
21. What was the worst quest you ever had?
22. What was your first job?
23. Would you rather give up cheese or oral sex?
24. What’s your home life? Do you have a partner? Children?
25. When was the last time you cried? Why?
26. What’s your favorite game?
27. Would you rather be famous while you’re alive and forgotten afterwards, or unknown during life and revered after death?
28. What’s one item at the top of your bucket list?
29. What’s your favorite alcoholic drink? Is there one you refuse to drink?
30. What is your greatest achievement?
31. What was the last dream you had?
32. Would you rather fight twelve child zombies or one zombie troll?
33. If a sorcerer transformed you into an animal, but you had a choice, what animal would you choose to become?
34. Is there any quest you would flatly refuse to do?
35. What’s the dumbest thing you’ve ever done?
36. What do you have in your pockets?
37. What would you do with 1,000g in your pocket right now?
38. What’s something you love about another guild member?
39. How many three-year-olds could you fight at once?
40. Do you have any scars? Where did you get them?
41. Would you rather be a vampire or a werewolf?
42. What’s your favorite joke?
43. What’s something you’re looking forward to?
44. What’s something you want?
45. What’s a secret that you know?
46. What’s the last thing you masturbated to?
47. When’s the first time you took a life?
48. What’s something you’d change about yourself?
49. Just how old are you anyway? When’s your birthday?
50. What is best in life?

sections.title: Running the City Phase
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> Social encounters in the City aren’t like social encounters in the Underworld. In the Underworld, the characters are invaders. In the City, characters are part of the ecosystem. That is a fundamentally different paradigm.

> [!lede]
> Through role-playing, the City blooms for the players. However, the players must find the appropriate keys for the gates that are placed in front of them. The GM’s job is threefold: **Find what goals the players have, clearly define what is needed to achieve those goals, and create interesting obstacles.**

sections.title: Seed and grow goals
sections.body:
In the earliest sessions of the game, a player might have no specific goals or desires in the City. That’s fine. However, as a GM, it’s your job to lure them into the web of intrigue that makes the City Phase especially interesting. This is done by clearly showing the resources, boons, and wish fulfillment that can be gained by interacting with the City factions.

Initially, players may be interested in simple things: more money and more power. Again—that’s fine. Use these incentives as lures to a world of actual intrigue. As players get embroiled in factional strife, different goals will begin to emerge from base needs.

As with the Underworld, the City should be bizarre and complex. The City creation rules in Appendix D are designed to be evocative and inspiring. The setting is an anti-canon. Throw out ideas that don’t work for your game. Jam other shit in there. The people in the City should be evocative, scary, funny, weird, and interesting. The organizations should feel both rooted in history and fantastic. As a hint, nothing you can come up with will be weirder than history already is. Read a lot, collect a lot of ideas, and mash them together into your City.

Broadcast all the districts and special City Actions available to your players. **Create a shared document detailing all the things players can** do in **the City**. This lets players make informed decisions.

Players will be obliged to take studious notes, draw relationship maps, track favors owed, keep journals about the various likes and dislikes of various GM characters, etc. Figuring out how to navigate the social situations of the City Phase replicates the fun of discovery found during the Crawl Phase.

sections.title: Create a path to success
sections.body:
Don’t be coy about how players might achieve their goals. It’s not actually fun to be mysterious: it engenders a sense of mistrust between the GM and the players. If a player can declare a clear goal, you can provide a clear path towards that goal.

The [[09 - Chapter 9 - The City Phase#Support|Support]] City Action is **the main tool that players have to make meaningful progress towards open-ended goals**. Create a consistent metric for how you set complexity when adventurers are performing the Support action. Be open-minded when players propose actions that tick off complexity.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
**Player:** I want to become the most respected mead maker in the City.

**GM:** OK. First, you have to actually build your meadery. That’s a Building action. “Meadery” is three syllables, so it’s going to take at least 150g to open your most basic, hole-in-the-wall joint. The fancier you want it to be, you can add more description for more money.

**Player:** I want it, literally, to be the “best meadery in the City.” That’s… eight syllables. So 400g.

**GM:** I agree. Then, you have to woo and court influential members of the aristocracy to hype your meadery. Starting complexity for basic tasks is at least complexity 3, but because being the best _anything_ in the City is difficult, let’s set the Support action to 5 complexity.

sections.title: Create obstacles
sections.body:
At the same time, you should make the paths to success fraught with peril. As the adventurers rise in the City, they’ll undoubtedly brush shoulders with powers that do not want any rivals. These rivals can **put** roadblocks in their way.

These dangers should not be easily perceived. Surprise setbacks are fair game; they test the players’ creativity and ability to react to new information.

Do not _unmake_ a player’s progress. If the GM burns down the meadery from the previous example, the player probably has good reason to be grumpy. Rather, introduce roadblocks.

For example, perhaps a rival bribes the tradesman’s union so that they will no longer do work for an adventurer—to use the Build action, the adventurer must get the union back on their side.

Importantly, the City is a place of laws. Murdering everything in the Underworld may be a strategy that gets results, but in the City it gets you jailed and executed. The players cannot kill their way out of social situations.

In general, we recommend not using the Challenge Phase rules at all in the City. If the players are contemplating some violence, reduce it to a Swords test. On a success, the players have won and can declare what sort of punishment they deal out: do they kill their opponent or simply slap them around a little? Depending on what damage is dealt and the relative social status of those involved, you can decide on the “appropriate” response from the All-Watch—the response from those in power is never commensurate.

sections.title: Completing quests and soft endings
sections.body:
The nature of the sandbox can make it tricky to know when the game is “over.” A more plot-driven game might be over when the players win or lose—the ring is cast into the fire, the Death Star is destroyed, everybody lives happily ever after. Not so in _His Majesty the Worm._ The players create their own quests and drive their own goals. When one adventurer’s quest is over, the rest of the guild still have quests to pursue.

An adventurer’s career ends in two ways: death or retirement. It should be the goal of every player to finish their adventurer’s quest and retire to safety in the City.

When one adventurer succeeds in their quest, it’s a good time to check in with your table.

- Do the players want to keep playing? Whose quest should they pursue next?

- Do the players want to continue playing _His Majesty the Worm_ but in a new setting? Should you all remake the City and Underworld (see Appendices D and E) and make a new guild?

- Does another player want to try their hand at GMing?

- Does the table want to play something else for a while? There’re tons of cool games out there.

You can keep playing _His Majesty the Worm_ or take a break. Just check in and make sure everybody is having as much fun as possible. The game might never be “over”—you can come back to the game again and again, creating a long and fondly-remembered history.

sections.title: Converting Other Games
sections.body: An advantage of **OSR** games is that it’s simple to convert between them. _His Majesty the Worm_ plays like an oldschool game but is not a retroclone. A little braingrease must be applied to convert rules, modules, and monsters into this game format, although it’s more of an art than a skill. Here are some guidelines.

sections.title: Player character stats
sections.body: Adventurers’ attribute ratings in _His Majesty the Worm_ are roughly equivalent to attribute bonuses in retroclone systems. For example, “Strength - 17 (+3)” would be “Swords 3.”

sections.title: OSR
sections.body:
| OSR | His Majesty the Worm |
|---|---|
| Strength bonus | Swords score |
| Dexterity bonus | Pentacles score |
| Wisdom bonus | Cups score |
| Charisma bonus | Wands score |
| Fighter | Path of Swords |
| Thief | Path of Pentacles |
| Cleric | Path of Cups |
| Magic-user | Path of Wands |
| Saving throws | Tests of fate |

sections.title: Monster stats
sections.body:
A retroclone monster’s **Hit Dice (HD) = their Health and Defense**. Monsters in _His Majesty the Worm_ are about as tough as in a retroclone.

Allocate the monster’s HD into a combination of Health or Defense. If a monster is very well armored (like a dragon), the Defense score will be higher. If a monster is very fast and hard to hit, the Health score will be higher. If you’re not sure, just make the monster’s Health and Defense roughly equivalent. For example, a 7HD dragon might have 2 Health, 5 Defense.

sections.title: Combat
sections.body:
“To-hit” and “damage” are mostly meaningless in _His Majesty the Worm._ A **Wound** is the average damage done by a single sword swing.

If a monster does an overwhelming amount of damage, you can represent that in different ways. A giant’s hammer might deal 2 Wounds, whereas a dragon’s unblockable fire breath might deal a Piercing Wound.

sections.title: Magic
sections.body:
When converting spells, first look for an equivalent spell in Appendix A. Feather Fall can be represented by the Feather spell, Cause Wounds can be represented by Withering, and so on.

Spells beyond the 2nd level might be beyond the scope of adventurer abilities in this game. If they are a core part of a monster’s move set, look at the [[01 - Chapter 1 - The Basics#Effects|Effects]] list and make a judgment about how best to represent that power here.

> [!epigraph]
> “How they will rejoice in passing from darkness to light! How worthless to them will seem the honours and glories of the den! But now imagine further, that they descend into their old habitations—in that underground dwelling they will not see as well as their fellows, and will not be able to compete with them in the measurement of the shadows on the wall; there will be many jokes about the man who went on a visit to the sun and lost his eyes, and if they find anybody trying to set free and enlighten one of their number, they will put him to death, if they can catch him.”
>
> _– “The Allegory of the Cave,” The Republic, Plato_

sections.title: Inspirational and Educational Reading
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> Here are some things that we think are awesome. _His Majesty the Worm_ wouldn’t exist without them. If you consume this media, you’ll get what we’re going for with this game.

sections.title: Core inspiration
sections.body: The central influences on _His Majesty the Worm_ all happen to be comics. Not sure why comics were the main inspiration here; something about the visual medium and the vaguely alternate aesthetic? We don't know!

sections.title: Dungeon Meshi by Ryoko Kui
sections.body:
Dungeon Meshi is the most thoughtful treatment of the physicality of dungeoneering that we've ever read. The characters, their gear, and their journeys have a practical weight. Its considerations of exploration, food, and exhaustion are fun and evocative. This should be required reading for anybody that wants to ignore mundane gear or avoid tracking rations.

You can run _His Majesty the Worm_ as a _Dungeon Meshi_ RPG if you swap the word “alchemy” for “cooking.”

sections.title: House of Orr by Nolan T. Jones, Rilley Dutton, and Richard Zayas and artist Victoria Grace Elliott
sections.body:
A defunct and unfinished webcomic that is currently super hard to find on the internet. As such, apologies for including it here.

That said, _House of Orr_ genuinely shaped our thinking about “the party as a character.” In the setting, political capital is held by adventuring guilds. A struggling guild, the titular House of Orr (who, by tradition, requires all members to take on a new name with the element “Orr”—Orrlock, Orrdalf, Orrwyn, etc.), hopes to establish itself as a political power. With its whimsical elements, _House of Orr_ is genuinely delightful. It evokes the sense of playfulness that we want a game of _His Majesty the Worm_ to have.

sections.title: I Roved Out In Search of Truth and Love by Alexis Flowers
sections.body:
A “warmly pornographic” comic. If you strip out all the pornography, you have a super fun fantasy story. If you strip out all the fantasy story, you have some damn good smut. It is humorous and beautiful in a way that we want a game of _His Majesty the Worm_ to be.

By default, _His Majesty the Worm_ isn't pornographic—that would require a lot of buy-in, consent tools, etc. It's not the sort of game we’re trying to run 99% of the time. It is, however, an “adult” game. Adventurers can buy into relationships with each other by electing the Lovers Bond.

sections.title: Rat Queens by Kurtis J. Wiebe and Roc Upchurch
sections.body:
Goddamn, _Rat Queens_ rules. The friendship and interactions between the _Rat Queens_ illustrates the inter-party relationships of _His Majesty the Worm._ We want every adventure to delve into each character’s motivations, backstory, and friendships in the same way that _Rat Queens_ does.

The one-two punches (e.g., the Betty Climber) that the _Rat Queens_ perform in combat are half the reason the Challenge system works the way it does, too. Aid each other in combat to get the **BIG** numbers.

sections.title: As Above, So Below
sections.body: A found footage film where archaeologists-cum-urban-explorers delve into the Paris catacombs. They find Templar tombs, treasure, out-of-place artifacts, demons, and doom. It’s a great example of having a mythic underworld sitting under a major metropolitan area.

sections.title: Cube
sections.body: A group of people wake up in a bizarre complex of interconnected cubes that are also death traps. Slowly, they start to piece together the puzzle of how to navigate them safely. A great example of how claustrophobic and terrifying crawling through a deathtrap dungeon would be.

sections.title: Indiana Jones
sections.body: The **pulp** content of the Indiana Jones movies makes them genre staples in terms of dungeon-crawling. Think about the cool traps in _Raiders of the Lost Ark_ or the puzzles in _The Last Crusade._ It’s rare to see such careful attention to dungeon-crawling deliberately called out in popular media.

sections.title: Labyrinth
sections.body: A young woman’s baby brother is trapped in the center of a sprawling maze by the Goblin King and she has until midnight to rescue him. As she adventures through the maze, she solves riddles, makes allies, and overcomes challenges. Dungeon-crawling at its most delightful.

sections.title: Spine of Night
sections.body: Although it’s not about dungeon crawling, the sheer inventiveness of its ultra-gory, heavy-metal aesthetic is hard to rival. It deals with brutal warriors, greedy scholars, winged assassins, and power-mad sorcerers delving into powers that mortals were not meant to know. Watch it and be inspired.

sections.title: House of Leaves by Mark Z. Danielewski
sections.body: Several narratives beautifully woven together: an academic critique of a found footage horror film, the personal journal of a man’s descent into schizophrenia, letters from a character’s mother. _House of Leaves_ plays with text in a way that few novels do. People say it’s weird but it’s honestly pretty gettable if you’re willing to give it a try.

sections.title: Invisible Cities by Italo Calvino
sections.body: Framed as a conversation between Marco Polo and Kublai Khan, _Invisible Cities_ lists fifty-five fictitious cities and their fictitious histories. As a meditation on memory, it is excellent, compelling the reader to search for hidden meanings in the text. It is an example of what is meant by the term “**anti-canon**.”

sections.title: Piranesi by Susanna Clarke
sections.body: The titular character lives (almost) alone in a museum world comprising three floors: a flooded basement, sprawling central corridors, and the occasional bird winging through the upper stories. An excellent example of what a mythic Underworld might feel like.

sections.title: Tombs of Atuan by Ursula K. LeGuin
sections.body:
In this novel, the main character is a priestess of the Old Powers. She tends a lightless labyrinth of tombs—a labyrinth with a dark, unknown purpose. Forty-percent of the story is told without the visual sense; this seems like an impossible task but is wildly successful.

Ultimately, this novel is one of the finest examples of fantasy fiction in the English language.

sections.title: Blogs
sections.body: _His Majesty the Worm_ suckled on the terrible, sweet milk that came out of the blogosphere during the nascence of the OSR movement. All posts listed below are online as of this printing.

sections.title: “Blorb Principles,” from Idiomdrottning by Sandra Snan
sections.body:
“Blorb” is a funny name given to a prep style that emphasizes preparing the game space thoroughly before players begin to interact with it. It advocates creating a robust setting up front so that the GM has to do very little (if any) improv during the game.

In order of precedence, blorb prioritizes: 1. Prep 2. Procedure 3. Ideas that fill in the gaps between prep and procedure

If this appeals to you, you will find a game type analogous to how _His Majesty the Worm_ was played during its seven years of playtesting.

**Link:** https://idiomdrottning.org/blorb-principles

sections.title: “Dungeon Checklist,” from Goblinpunch by Arnold K
sections.body:
This is an excellent tool to use while building dungeons, and served as an inspiration for our own checklist in Appendix E.

**Link:** http://goblinpunch.blogspot.com/2016/01/ dungeon-checklist.html

sections.title: “The Dungeon as Mythic Underworld,” from Philotomy’s Musings by Jason Cone
sections.body:
Philotomy’s Musings is a collection of interpretive essays about OD&D that contained a revolutionary way to re-imagine megadungeons. The way it frames a dungeon as an inherently mythic space served as an inspiration for the core setting of this game.

**Link:** https://save.vs.totalpartykill.ca/grab-bag/ philotomy/ (rehosted with permission)

sections.title: “Handling IC Nastiness,” from Cavegirl’s Game Stuff by Emily Allen
sections.body:
An essay on handling out-of-character traumas and phobias in an honest, collaborative way without using tools that might make players feel **put** in a spot.

**Link:** http://cavegirlgames.blogspot.com/2019/02/ handling-ic-nastiness.html

sections.title: “The ICI Doctrine: Information, Choice, Impact,” from Bastionland by Chris McDowall
sections.body:
This essay articulates that creating a true sense of player agency is done by emphasizing information, choice, and impact. This is a fundamental text to understand how to best organize the conversation of role-playing games from a GM’s perspective.

**Link:** https://www.bastionland.com/2018/09/the-icidoctrine-information-choice.html

sections.title: “Landmark, Hidden, Secret” from DIY & Dragons by Anne
sections.body:
Inspiration for the way that _His Majesty the Worm_ doles out information is drawn directly from this blog post. The post places all information on a continuum, from landmark (obvious) to hidden (requires cursory investigation) to secret (difficult to find).

**Link:** https://diyanddragons.blogspot.com/2019/10/ landmark-hidden-secret.html

sections.title: “In Corpathium,” from Last Gasp Grimoire by Logan Knight
sections.body:
The DNA of the City-creation rules in Appendix D are drawn from Logan Knight’s “Corpathium” setting.

**Link:** https://www.lastgaspgrimoire.com/in-corpathium/

sections.title: “Same Page Tool,” from Deeper in the Game by Christopher Chinn
sections.body:
The Same Page Tool is a great resource to help players and GMs understand what they want to get out of the game. It will be an asset while running session 0 and bringing new players into the game.

**Link:** https://bankuei.wordpress.com/2010/03/27/the-same-page-tool/

sections.title: “TFP DMG: How I Use Skills,” from Polemic, 10’ by James Young
sections.body:
A treatise on how to adjudicate tests of fate. The post argues that adventurers are competent and their skills (or motifs, in this game’s paradigm) should let them do crazy things. Call for tests of fate only when the adventurers are trying to go above and beyond.

**Link:** http://tenfootpolemic.blogspot.com/2017/01/dmshit-how-i-use-skills.html

sections.title: Appendix A: Sorcery
sections.body:
> [!epigraph]
> “‘Dalla told me something once. Val's sister, Mance Rayder's wife. She said that sorcery was a sword without a hilt. There is no safe way to grasp it.’ ‘A wise woman.’ Melisandre rose, her red robes stirring in the wind. ‘A sword without a hilt is still a sword, though, and a sword is a fine thing to have when foes are all about.’”
>
> _– A Storm of Swords, George R. R. Martin_

Humans know that they are experiencing only a narrow band of reality. Their dogs can smell scents that their noses cannot. Their cats can see through darkness their eyes cannot penetrate. They know that to some things they are truly blind. And that is terrifying.  

Just beyond the bounds of **human** perception **there** are different worlds, different realities. And sometimes—just sometimes—forces from these realms will cross the threshold and actually enter our world.  

These intrusions are never subtle. Just like water and oil reject each other, the realms of men and the realms of spirits are anathema to the other. When they interact, the universe itself is warped and torn with the wrongness of it all. That is terrifying, too.  

Some people, however, willingly participate in this cosmic blasphemy. They seek to see beyond the veil of this world. They open the door to the things that lurk on the threshold and offer them entrance.  

These people are sorcerers. Nobody likes them.

sections.title: The Far Realms
sections.body:
> [!lede]
> There are four realms of spirits, sometimes called the “far realms,” that are tangent to the plane of Flesh, where men and dwarves and dogs and cows and all other mortal creatures live. These are called the Wastes, the Weald, the Weird, and the Welkin. All magic has its origin in one of these realms.

sections.title: The Wastes
sections.body: The **Wastes** are a barren place. It is dead. It is death. It is a place of grey skies and miasmic fens stretching to the horizon, scattered with piles of bones from wars that were ancient before the creation of the mortal world.

sections.title: Wastes spells
sections.body:
Brainfever  
Control Undead   
Darklight   
Fear  
Fleshcraft   
Malediction   
Necromancy   
Raise Zombie   
Stinking Cloud   
Withering

sections.title: The Weald
sections.body: The Weald is a wild place. It is alive. It is chaos. It is a place of twisting vines tangled together down into impossibly **deep** roots, and spreading branches stretching up into formless and churning storm clouds.

sections.title: Weald spells
sections.body:
Control Animal  
Defy Depths   
Flare   
Gust of Wind   
Protection from Elements   
Speak to Animal   
Thunderclap   
Totem   
Wall of Elements   
Woodweave

sections.title: The Weird
sections.body: The **Weird** is an ever-changing place. It is dream. It is madness. The realm of Weird is half allegory and half nonsense. Dreamers sometimes visit the Weird when they sleep; prophets live half in the Weird and half in the realm of Flesh.

sections.title: Weird spells
sections.body:
Animate Object  
Change Size  
Enrage  
Give Form to Nothingness  
Illusion  
Mirror Meld   
Portable Hole   
Scry   
Shroud   
Sleep

sections.title: The Welkin
sections.body: The Welkin is a bright and terrible place. It is order. It is law. It’s a place of blue skies and rainbow bridges leading to cloud cities where winged women bring mead to ancestor kings, who wage endless battles in preparation for the apocalypse.

sections.title: Welkin spells
sections.body:
Augury  
Binding   
Charm   
Circle of Protection   
Feather   
Guardian Angel   
Heavenfire   
Life   
Seal Pact   
Veritas

sections.title: Casting Spells
sections.body:
When energy from one of the far realms enters the **plane** of Flesh, it burns our reality, causing a strange, unpredictable, and violent reaction. This is called a spell.  

Sorcerers deal in spells. They make study of them, learn them, trade them, and use them. You may cast spells if you have one of the “**Magic of the**…” talents from the Path of Wands.  

Spells are summoned into our world by use of representational and iconic objects, called **components**.
